title: Claude Prompting in Practice
summary: This intermediate module enables learners to define success criteria, test prompts systematically, and improve Claude prompts with clear instructions, examples, and structured context. After completing it, learners can diagnose a prompt problem and select a documented prompting technique instead of revising by guesswork.
objectives: Define observable success criteria before revising a Claude prompt.
Write clear, direct, and ordered instructions for a task.
Use examples to demonstrate the output behavior a prompt should produce.
Separate instructions, context, examples, and input with consistent XML tags.
Compare prompt revisions against the same test cases and success criteria.

sections.title: Start with success criteria
paragraphs: Prompt improvement begins by defining what a successful response must accomplish and how that success will be tested. Observable criteria might address whether required information is present, whether the requested format is followed, and whether prohibited content is absent.

Create representative test inputs before comparing revisions. Run the original prompt and each revised prompt against the same inputs, then evaluate every response with the same criteria. Keeping the test conditions stable helps distinguish a useful prompt change from variation between unrelated tests.

Prompt editing is not always the right intervention. If the failure comes from missing information, an unsuitable task definition, or a requirement that cannot be evaluated, changing only the wording of the prompt does not resolve the underlying problem.

sections.title: Write clear and direct instructions
paragraphs: State the task explicitly, provide the context needed to perform it, and describe relevant constraints. Do not rely on Claude to infer an important requirement that could have been written directly.

When steps must happen in a particular sequence, present them as ordered instructions. Distinguish required behavior from optional guidance, and name the expected output format when format is part of the success criteria.

A practical revision process is to locate an observed failure, identify the missing or ambiguous instruction connected to that failure, and change only the relevant part of the prompt. Test the revision against the same cases before making additional changes.

sections.title: Demonstrate desired behavior with examples
paragraphs: Examples can demonstrate the relationship between an input and the desired output. They are useful when a verbal instruction alone does not fully communicate the expected format, tone, classification boundary, or decision pattern.

Choose examples that represent the behavior being evaluated. Keep their structure consistent, and ensure that the examples follow the written instructions rather than contradicting them. A contradictory example makes it unclear which behavior the prompt requires.
Examples do not replace success criteria. After adding or changing examples, evaluate the resulting responses against the same explicit requirements used for other revisions.

sections.title: Separate prompt components
paragraphs: Consistent XML tags can separate instructions, context, examples, and the input to be processed. Clear boundaries help identify which text states the task and which text is data for that task.

Use descriptive tag names consistently within the prompt. The purpose is structural clarity, not decoration. If a simple prompt already has unambiguous boundaries, adding more structure without an identified need may not improve it.
After restructuring a prompt, repeat the established tests. A structure change is successful only when it improves performance against the defined criteria.

sections.title: Iterate systematically
paragraphs: Change one relevant element at a time when practical. Record the observed failure, the revision, and the test result. This makes it easier to connect an outcome to a particular change.

Select a technique based on the failure. Add a missing direct instruction when a requirement is unstated, use ordered instructions when sequence is unclear, add examples when the desired behavior needs demonstration, and introduce tags when prompt components are difficult to distinguish.

Retain a revision only when the test results support it. If results do not improve, restore the prior wording or investigate whether the success criteria, supplied context, or task definition need attention.

questions.prompt: What should a learner establish before comparing prompt revisions?
choices: Observable success criteria and representative test inputs
A different test input for every revision
As many simultaneous wording changes as possible
questions.explanation: The module teaches learners to define observable success criteria and representative test inputs before comparing revisions under stable test conditions.

questions.prompt: When are ordered instructions most appropriate?
choices: When the steps must occur in a particular sequence
When the task has no required sequence
When success criteria have not been defined
When replacing every example in a prompt
questions.explanation: The clear-instructions section says to present steps as ordered instructions when they must happen in a particular sequence.

questions.prompt: What is the primary role of examples in the process taught by this module?
choices: To demonstrate the relationship between an input and the desired output
To eliminate the need for written instructions and success criteria
To make the test inputs different for each revision
To prove that every response will be correct
questions.explanation: The examples section teaches that examples demonstrate desired behavior, while written instructions, success criteria, and testing remain necessary.

questions.prompt: Why might a learner add consistent XML tags to a prompt?
choices: To separate instructions, context, examples, and input clearly
To avoid testing the revised prompt
To guarantee that every response meets the criteria
questions.explanation: The structure section teaches that consistent XML tags can create clear boundaries between different prompt components.
